items.readable_text:
Content:
We can also complete the square to integrate hyperbolic arcsecant, arccosecant, and arccotangent.

Content:
For example, let's consider the integral

Content:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{\left(x+3\right)\sqrt{-x^2-6x}} \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
As it is, this integral doesn't resemble any of the basic integrals we have encountered so far. However, we can complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: − x^{2} − 6x|= − (x^{2} + 6x); = − (x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 3x + 3^{2} − 3^{2}); = − ((x + 3)^{2} − 9); = 9 − (x + 3)^{2}]

Content:
If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of [MATH: 9] under the square root, we get

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/((x + 3)sqrt(− x^{2} − 6x))dx|= ∫(1)/((x + 3)sqrt(9 − (x + 3)^{2}))dx; = ∫(1)/(3(x + 3)sqrt(1 − ((x + 3)/(3))^{2}))dx; = (1)/(9)∫(1)/(((x + 3)/(3))sqrt(1 − ((x + 3)/(3))^{2}))dx.]

Content:
This now looks more familiar! Let [MATH: u = \dfrac {x+3}{3}.] Then

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 3\,\textrm{d}u.]

Content:
We can now write the integral as

Content:
[MATH: ∫(1)/((x + 3)sqrt(− x^{2} − 6x))dx|= (1)/(9)∫(1)/(((x + 3)/(3))sqrt(1 − ((x + 3)/(3))^{2}))dx; = (1)/(9)∫(1)/(usqrt(1 − u^{2})) ⋅ (3du); = (1)/(3)∫(1)/(usqrt(1 − u^{2}))du.]

Content:
This is a basic integral for an inverse reciprocal hyperbolic function, and we can solve it in one step:
[MATH: \newcommand{\arsinh}{\mathop{\rm arsinh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcosh}{\mathop{\rm arcosh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\artanh}{\mathop{\rm artanh}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\sech}{\mathop{\rm sech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\csch}{\mathop{\rm csch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\coth}{\mathop{\rm coth}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arsech}{\mathop{\rm arsech}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcsch}{\mathop{\rm arcsch}\nolimits}
\newcommand{\arcoth}{\mathop{\rm arcoth}\nolimits}]

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(3)∫(1)/(usqrt(1 − u^{2}))du|= − (1)/(3)arsech u + C; = − (1)/(3)arsech ((x + 3)/(3)) + C.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we note that [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{4-4(x-1)^2}\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - (x-1)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x-1.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore, [MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − (x − 1)^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ arcoth u + C; = (1)/(4)arcoth (x − 1) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|{x-1} \right| > 1.]

items.title: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: [MATH: \eqalign{ 2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 2x)\[5pt] & = -(x^2 - 2\cdot x + 1^2-1^2)\[5pt] & = -((x-1)^2 - 1) \[5pt] &= 1 - (x-1)^2 }]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt { 1-(x-1)^2 } } \, \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x-1.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∫(1)/((x − 1)sqrt(2x − x^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/((x − 1)sqrt(1 − (x − 1)^{2}))dx; = ∫(1)/(usqrt(1 − u^{2}))du; = − arsech u + C; = − arsech (x − 1) + C.]

items.title: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

[MATH: x^{2} + 6x + 10|= x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 3x + 3^{2} − 3^{2} + 10; = (x + 3)^{2} + 1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{6}{|3x\!+\!9|\sqrt{x^2\!+\!6x\!+\!10}} \,\textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{6}{3|x\!+\!3|\sqrt {1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2} } \, \textrm{d}x = {2} \int \dfrac{1}{|x\!+\!3|\sqrt{1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x+3.] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: 2∫(1)/(|x + 3|sqrt(1 + (x + 3)^{2}))dx|= 2∫(1)/(|u|sqrt(1 + u^{2}))du; = − 2arcsch u + C; = − 2arcsch (x + 3) + C.]

items.title: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the denominator: [MATH: \eqalign{ 3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\[5pt] & = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\[5pt] & = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \[5pt] &= 4 - (x+1)^2 }]

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1).] Then, we have [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore, [MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − ((1)/(2)(x + 1))^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2})du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ arcoth u + C; = (1)/(2) ⋅ arcoth ((1)/(2)(x + 1)) + C; = (1)/(2)arcoth ((x + 1)/(2)) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|\dfrac {x+1} {2} \right| > 1.]

Item 2 — Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2} \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we note that
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-4(x-1)^2}\textrm{d}x =
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - (x-1)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x-1.] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,
[MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − (x − 1)^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ du; = (1)/(4) ⋅ arcoth u + C; = (1)/(4)arcoth (x − 1) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|{x-1} \right| > 1.]

Item 5 — Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x= }]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:
[MATH: \eqalign{
2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 2x)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 - 2\cdot x + 1^2-1^2)\[5pt]
& = -((x-1)^2 - 1) \[5pt]
&= 1 - (x-1)^2
}]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt { 1-(x-1)^2 } }	\, \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x-1.] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: ∫(1)/((x − 1)sqrt(2x − x^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/((x − 1)sqrt(1 − (x − 1)^{2}))dx; = ∫(1)/(usqrt(1 − u^{2}))du; = − arsech u + C; = − arsech (x − 1) + C.]

Item 8 — Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {\displaystyle \int \dfrac{6}{|3x+9|\sqrt{x^2+6x+10}} \textrm{d}x= }]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

[MATH: x^{2} + 6x + 10|= x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 3x + 3^{2} − 3^{2} + 10; = (x + 3)^{2} + 1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get
[MATH: \int \dfrac{6}{|3x\!+\!9|\sqrt{x^2\!+\!6x\!+\!10}} \,\textrm{d}x = \int \dfrac{6}{3|x\!+\!3|\sqrt {1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2} }	\, \textrm{d}x = {2} \int \dfrac{1}{|x\!+\!3|\sqrt{1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = x+3.] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,

[MATH: 2∫(1)/(|x + 3|sqrt(1 + (x + 3)^{2}))dx|= 2∫(1)/(|u|sqrt(1 + u^{2}))du; = − 2arcsch u + C; = − 2arcsch (x + 3) + C.]

Item 11 — Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2} \textrm{d}x=]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:
[MATH: \eqalign{
3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\[5pt]
& = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \[5pt]
&= 4 - (x+1)^2
}]

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x =
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.]

Let [MATH: u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1).] Then, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Therefore,
[MATH: (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − ((1)/(2)(x + 1))^{2})dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 − u^{2})du; = (1)/(2) ⋅ arcoth u + C; = (1)/(2) ⋅ arcoth ((1)/(2)(x + 1)) + C; = (1)/(2)arcoth ((x + 1)/(2)) + C.]

Note that this result is subject to the condition [MATH: \left|\dfrac {x+1} {2} \right| > 1.]
